messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Media / News: Related news, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elena Morales is a 70-year-old fashion designer who has spent most of her adult life working with fabric in close, tactile ways, draping cloth over forms, pinning hems, and moving between steam, pressing tables, and bolts of material in her studio. The trauma she returns to began two years ago, when she witnessed a fatal crowd crush outside a downtown venue after a winter charity gala where one of her oldest friends had been attending. Elena had been only a few steps away when the exit bottlenecked and panic spread. She remembers the abrupt cold against her forearms as the doors opened to the night air, the press of bodies, the helplessness of seeing her friend go down and disappear from view while people shouted and surged. She had reached forward but could not get to her. In the aftermath, no one was charged. Elena has come to believe, with painful certainty, that the people responsible faced no real consequences, and that what happened occurred because of the way she acted in those seconds: if she had moved faster, shouted louder, pulled harder, she tells herself, she should have protected her friend and failed.

Since then, the memory does not stay in the past. It forces its way into her mind without her consent, and when it comes, it arrives whole. A draft of cold air across her skin in the studio, the chill from an over-air-conditioned fitting room, even stepping from a heated car into winter weather can bring back not just an image but the full scene with terrifying immediacy: the metallic smell, the sound of people yelling, the sensation of bodies pushing, the sight of her friend’s face. Sometimes a news segment about a crowd incident or public disaster does the same thing. She is not thinking about the event beforehand; something in the surroundings simply ignites it, and for a moment it feels completely real again. What frightens Elena is how little warning there is. She can be arranging a sleeve on a mannequin and, with a change in temperature on her skin, she is back at that doorway.

Those moments also pull her toward the same harsh conclusions. When she sees coverage of another preventable tragedy, she becomes consumed not only by anger that those responsible so often seem untouched, but by the conviction that her own failure is being replayed in front of her. The trigger is never just a reminder; it becomes proof, in her mind, that she did not do enough. Even situations that involve a simple loss of control—production delays, a model arriving late, a fitting that runs off schedule—have become strangely potent. The feeling that events are no longer in her hands resembles the worst instant of that night closely enough that she braces, and her mind rushes to the same accusations against herself.

Over time, those beliefs have made the memory even harder to contain. Because Elena is certain she failed to protect someone she loved, the memory returns with a punishing quality, as if her mind will not allow her to look away from the evidence. Each uncontrolled reliving seems to confirm her self-blame all over again. After an episode she can spend hours going over tiny details—where she stood, when she reached, whether one different movement would have changed the outcome. In this way the memory and her judgments about it have become tightly bound: the more vividly it intrudes, the more certain she feels of her guilt, and the more her guilt seems to call the scene back.

Her efforts to manage this have gradually narrowed her life. She no longer watches the news because footage of disasters, even brief headlines overheard in a showroom, can set everything off. She avoids memorial gatherings and even ordinary reminders of the friend she lost, including certain fabrics they used to shop for together, because grief feels too dangerous; once she lets herself feel it, she fears the entire night will break open again. She has also begun pushing away moments of warmth and pleasure with her husband and adult children. If she catches herself laughing over dinner or feeling proud after finishing a design, she goes flat and withdrawn, as if positive feeling itself were unsafe. In her mind, letting go for even a moment means losing control, and loss of control is exactly what her body and mind now register as danger.

These strategies have reached into her work. Elena has started keeping the studio overheated and asks assistants to handle client fittings in colder rooms. She avoids industry chatter when major events are in the news and leaves the radio off. Yet this shrinking of her world has made her more vigilant, not less. The colder corner of a workroom, a phone screen with a breaking-news banner, the small unpredictability of a hectic production day all stand out to her more sharply now, as if she is scanning for the next ambush. By trying so hard not to be caught off guard, she has become more sensitive to exactly the things that catch her.

Her husband finally urged her to seek help after he found her trembling in the studio one morning, clutching a coat sleeve because a burst of cold air from an open service door had brought the whole scene back with such force that she could not tell, for several seconds, where she was. Elena came in exhausted and ashamed. What she fears most is that she will remain trapped in that doorway for the rest of her life, still to blame, still unable to protect the person she lost. What she hopes, more quietly, is that she might one day remember her friend without being dragged back into the moment she could not stop.
